mcqs.q: What can generative AI do that a normal calculator cannot?
o: create brand-new text, images or music
add a long list of numbers
work out long sums very fast
show the answer on a small screen
mcqs.e: Generative AI produces brand-new content based on patterns it learned; the other options are ordinary computer tasks.

mcqs.q: You want a clearer answer from a chatbot. Which change to your typed request (your prompt) helps most?
o: repeat the same request several times
add a role, a clear task and a limit
make the request as short as possible
write the whole request in capitals
mcqs.e: A prompt works best with a role, a specific task and a constraint; vague prompts give vague answers.

mcqs.q: A chatbot like a Large Language Model mainly works by…
o: storing every possible answer in a database
following a fixed set of grammar rules
searching the live web for each reply
predicting the next likely word, step by step
mcqs.e: An LLM predicts the next word again and again, using patterns from huge amounts of text.

mcqs.q: AI systems learn their skills mainly from…
o: a single built-in fixed rule
random guessing each time
advice from one human expert
lots of example data
mcqs.e: AI learns patterns from training data. The data shapes what it can and cannot do.

mcqs.q: An AI turns words into number-lists (vectors) so that words with similar meanings get…
o: completely random numbers
the same number as every other word
similar numbers, sitting close together
no numbers at all
mcqs.e: Similar meanings get similar numbers - the idea behind embeddings.

mcqs.q: To sort fruit photos into groups when no names are given, the AI looks for…
o: shared features such as colour and shape
the name of the photographer
the date each file was saved
the order they were uploaded
mcqs.e: Grouping by shared features is how unlabelled data is organised.

mcqs.q: A robot dog earns a point each time it takes a step without falling, and loses a point when it falls. After many tries it walks smoothly. How did it learn?
o: by copying a rule book written by its makers
by memorising a video of another robot walking
by asking its owner before every single step
by trial and error, keeping the actions that earned rewards
mcqs.e: Learning from rewards by trial and error is called reinforcement learning - moves that earn points get repeated, and moves that lose points get dropped.

mcqs.q: A shocking video shows a real politician saying something they never said; it was AI-made. Before reacting, the wise step is to…
o: share it immediately so others see it
check whether it is a genuine clip from a trusted source
assume it is real because it looks real
add your own caption and repost it
mcqs.e: AI-made fakes of real people (deepfakes) can look convincing; verify with trusted sources before believing or sharing.

mcqs.q: You sketch an AI “homework checker”. A sensible FAILURE to plan for - with a fix - is…
o: it confuses two pupils' similar handwriting; fix: ban handwriting
it works slowly at busy times; fix: skip the checking step
it marks a messy but correct answer wrong; fix: allow human review
it needs many example answers; fix: train it on none
mcqs.e: Naming a likely failure and a fix (human review) is good design.

mcqs.q: You use AI to make a picture, then enter it in an art contest as if you drew it yourself. This is mainly a problem of…
o: the image resolution chosen
the colour balance settings
honesty and giving credit
the saved file format
mcqs.e: Being honest about AI’s help matters. Claiming AI work as fully your own is unfair to others.

mcqs.q: These examples follow one rule. Work out the rule, then give the output for 10.
mcqs.e: Each output is double the input minus one (2→3, 3→5, 4→7), so 10→19. Inferring a rule from examples and applying it to a new input is the core idea behind machine learning.

mcqs.q: Follow the rules. RULE 1: if a word has the letter ‘z’, score 2. RULE 2: if it is longer than 4 letters, score 1. Word: “pizza”. Total score?
mcqs.e: 2 + 1 = 3. Adding up rule points step by step is how a simple AI scores things.

mcqs.q: An AI agent is different from a plain chatbot because it can…
o: store far more of your past conversations
reply with much longer, more detailed messages
run without needing any electricity at all
plan steps and use tools to reach a goal
mcqs.e: An agent plans, takes actions and can use tools (like searching or a calculator) to finish a task.

mcqs.q: Which is the SAFEST thing to paste into a public chatbot?
o: Your friend’s home address
A made-up practice question
A family member’s password
A classmate’s medical note
mcqs.e: Never share private information about yourself or others. Made-up practice content is fine.

mcqs.q: Before trusting an important fact from AI, you should…
o: repeat it so you remember it
share it with your classmates
check it against a reliable source
save it as a screenshot
mcqs.e: AI can be wrong, so verify important facts with a trusted source.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between classifying and generating?
o: Classifying sorts items; generating makes new content
Both simply mean creating brand-new pictures
Classifying writes text while generating deletes it
They are two different names for the same thing
mcqs.e: Classification labels/sorts existing things; generation creates new things.

mcqs.q: Which prompt is likely to give the BEST result?
o: “Write a poem about an animal.”
“Make a cat poem, any length is fine.”
“Do a nice poem for me, please and thanks.”
“Write a funny 4-line poem about a sleepy cat.”
mcqs.e: A specific, clear prompt (topic, length, style, audience) gives better generative results than a vague one.

mcqs.q: Some artists are upset that AI learned from their drawings without asking. This is a debate about…
o: fairness and consent for training data
the layout of the app's menus
the speed of the internet
which file format to use
mcqs.e: Who owns the data AI learns from, and whether permission was given, is a real ethical debate.

mcqs.q: Does a chatbot truly “understand” your words the way a human friend does?
o: Yes, exactly like a human friend does
Yes, it genuinely feels real emotions
No, it only predicts language patterns
Only for very simple, everyday questions
mcqs.e: AI matches patterns in language. It does not understand or feel as people do.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a real-world cost of training a big AI model?
o: it wears out the user's keyboard
it uses large amounts of electricity and water
it uses up the internet's words
it makes other computers run slower worldwide
mcqs.e: Training and serving big models runs on data centres that draw electricity and cooling water - a real cost someone pays.

mcqs.q: You read an amazing online story “written by a student.” A clue it might be AI-made is that it…
o: was posted on the site fairly recently
is neatly divided into several paragraphs
has a clear, descriptive title at the top
is polished yet gets simple facts wrong
mcqs.e: AI text can read smoothly yet contain made-up facts or a generic tone - stay curious and check.

mcqs.q: A tiny “points machine” decides if an email is spam. +3 if it says “free prize”, +2 if it has many links, −1 if from a known friend. Email: “FREE PRIZE!! click these links” from a stranger. Score?
mcqs.byhand: RULES: +3 “free prize” · +2 many links · −1 known friend
mcqs.e: 3 + 2 = 5. A higher score means “more likely spam.” You computed a simple model yourself.

mcqs.q: You have checked carefully and are now SURE a shocking video of a classmate is an AI-made fake. The responsible next step is to…
o: repost it with a warning caption
report it to a trusted adult or the platform
keep a copy to show friends later
do nothing - fakes are harmless
mcqs.e: When you find a harmful fake, report it so it can be taken down. Spreading it further - even with a warning - still increases the harm.

mcqs.q: Generative AI can also help programmers by…
o: guaranteeing the code has no mistakes
finding every bug with no human checking
drafting code for a person to check and test
running finished code faster
mcqs.e: AI can draft code, but humans must still check and test it.

mcqs.q: When a voice assistant hears you speak, turning the sound into words it can work with happens in its…
o: acting step
sensing step
reward step
sleeping step
mcqs.e: Hearing and converting your speech is the agent's sense step - input first, then think, then act.

mcqs.q: Who often prepares the labelled examples that AI learns from?
o: the model invents all labels itself
people who label the data manually
labels are copied automatically online
no labels are needed at all
mcqs.e: People label data (e.g., “this is a cat”), so human choices shape the AI.

mcqs.q: Your friend wants to ask a chatbot for medical advice about a real illness. The wisest thing is to…
o: fully trust the chatbot’s diagnosis
see a doctor; AI is not a substitute
ask it exactly which medicine to take
just wait and see if it passes on its own
mcqs.e: For health, money or safety, rely on qualified people. AI can give wrong or unsafe answers.

mcqs.q: A GOOD use of AI that helps people is…
o: describing images for the blind
writing fake product reviews for money
automatically liking all your own posts
secretly copying answers during a test
mcqs.e: AI can improve accessibility, such as describing images for blind users - a positive use.

mcqs.q: A face-recognition tool works well for some people but makes more mistakes for others. This shows the importance of…
o: using much higher-resolution cameras
training the staff to type much faster
adding several more display screens
testing AI for fairness
mcqs.e: AI should be tested for fairness so it does not disadvantage some groups.

mcqs.q: The most responsible way to use generative AI for schoolwork is to…
o: hand in its output as if it were your own work
use it but never bother to fact-check what it says
learn from it, then verify
let it complete your entire exam for you
mcqs.e: Responsible use = learn, verify, and be honest about AI’s help.

structured.title: Task 1 · Build a “Points Machine” from First Principles
structured.scenario:
A school wants a simple AI to flag possibly unkind messages for a teacher to check. The “points machine” gives each message a score:
• +3 if it contains a mean name
• +2 if it is in ALL CAPITAL LETTERS
• +1 if it has 3 or more “!”
• −2 if the sender often sends kind messages

Flag a message if the score is 3 or more.
parts: a) Score this message from a usually-kind sender: “YOU ARE A LOSER!!!”  Show your working.
b) Should the message be flagged? Explain using your score.
c) The machine flags a message that was actually a joke between best friends. Why can a simple rule machine make this mistake, and why should a human still check before anyone is punished?

model.text: +3 (mean name “loser”) +2 (ALL CAPS) +1 (3 “!”) −2 (kind sender) = 4. (2 marks per correct rule applied.)
model.rationale: Rewards executing a scoring model step by step and combining positive and negative weights correctly.

model.text: Yes - 4 is ≥ 3, so it is flagged for a teacher to look at.
model.rationale: Checks the learner applies the decision threshold, the core of a simple classifier.

model.text: The machine only counts words/CAPS; it cannot understand tone, friendship or jokes (context). So it gives false positives. A human should make the final call so no one is unfairly punished by a rule that missed the meaning.
model.rationale: Surfaces the key dilemma: automated systems lack context and can be unfair, so meaningful human oversight protects people.

structured.totalNote: Full marks: correct score (a), correct flag decision (b), and a clear explanation of why human oversight matters (c).

structured.title: Task 2 · Design a Responsible Homework-Helper Agent
structured.scenario:
An AI agent can sense a request, plan steps, use tools (like a calculator or web search), and act to help reach a goal.

Design a generative-AI “study buddy” agent whose goal is to help a Grade 5 student learn, not to do the work for them.
parts: a) List two tools your agent could use and what each is for.
b) Write the agent’s plan as 3–4 steps for helping with a maths question (sense → plan → act).
c) Dilemma: The student types, “Just give me all the answers to my graded test so I can copy them.” What should a responsible study-buddy do and say, and why?

model.text: Any two sensible tools, e.g., a calculator (to check arithmetic) and a search/reference tool (to find an explanation or example). (2 marks each.)
model.rationale: Tests understanding that agents extend their abilities with external tools rather than ‘knowing everything’.

model.text: e.g., 1) Sense/read the question; 2) Plan: break it into steps; 3) Act: guide the student with hints and one worked example; 4) Check the student’s answer and give feedback. (2 marks per clear stage.)
model.rationale: Rewards a genuine sense→plan→act loop aimed at teaching, not just outputting an answer.

model.text: It should decline to hand over graded-test answers and explain why (that would be cheating and would stop real learning). Instead it offers to teach the method, give practice questions, or hints. A good answer notes honesty/academic integrity and that the helper’s goal is learning.
model.rationale: A real dilemma between being ‘helpful’ and being ethical. Strong answers show the agent must refuse harm and redirect toward legitimate help - early alignment thinking.

structured.totalNote: Full marks: useful tools (a), a teaching-focused agent loop (b), and a principled refusal with a helpful alternative (c).
